Latest Valve Data Puts Steam Linux Marketshare At 0.90%

Although I've seen this metric previously, I still find it startling and a cause for alarm. Valve has put a LOT of resources into it's push to drag PC gaming over to Linux. It is incontrovertible that SteamOS has been an abject failure, as have Steam Machines. But the fact that Linux usage still only accounts for less than 1% is proof positive that they have made absolutely zero headway into bringing people over to Linux.

Why is this important? Because Valve put an awful lot of eggs in the Linux basket. Gabe flipped his shit with his tirades against Microsoft when he realized they might attempt to compete with Steam. His response was to throw millions upon millions of dollars and tons of resources to move PC gaming over to Linux where he could maintain his near virtual monopoly. It is clear now that this was foolish. Gamers did not move to Linux and having a non-growing sub 1% market share isn't likely to entice developers to invest resources porting games.

Although once so popular he was a meme, there are ample reasons to distrust Gabe Newell and Valve. His anti-Windows tirade was clearly motivated by his desire to continue Steam's virtual monopoly and not fact-based. It shouldn't be forgotten that Steam attempted to monetize "mods" and have taken a number of anti-consumer/anti-gamer positions. Then there are the "Steam Machines" that Valve touted as the future of PC gaming. These devices were intended to help propel their fork of Linux into the mainstream. Ultimately, it became clear that Valve's vision for the future of PC gaming looked nearly identical to console gaming, was more expensive, had a super-buggy OS, and was just plain shitty.

And then there's Linux. Steam OS and other varieties. This was going to be Gabe's big play--he was so pissed off that Steam might actually face some competition from Microsoft opening a gaming store that he was single-handily going to entice PC gamers and developers over to Linux where Steam could retain their virtual monopoly. Think about this--was Linux a demonstrably more capable platform? No, it was not. Was Linux more user-friendly? Absolutely it was not; to the contrary, unlike other modern OSs, Linux still requires users to drop to a command-line interface to do basic tasks ESPECIALLY TO GET GAMES RUNNING. Regardless of how you feel about Linux, it is fair to say that the learning curve can be steep if you need to do more than just very basic tasks. Was any of this in the interest of gamers? Absolutely not. As the numbers prove, >99% have no problem with gaming on Windows. It is a rock-solid platform. There are no problems, perceived or otherwise. Now some might argue, "what's wrong with having a choice?" Generally speaking, having a "choice" is great--but let's be intellectually honest--Valve hasn't invested all that money and resources into SteamOS, Steam Machines, and coaxing developers to develop for Linux to give a statistically insignificant number of people a "choice." It did so in an attempt to preserve a virtual anti-consumer monopoly and their plan involved moving to an inferior platform and transforming PC gaming into a console-like experience.
